title: Needle lace bars
subtitle: Buttonhole-covered bars that bridge the spaces in Richelieu cutwork before the background is cut away
excerpt: Needle lace bars are the connecting bridges of Richelieu cutwork embroidery. Before the background fabric is cut away, bars of thread are laid across each space and covered with closely-worked buttonhole stitches to make them firm and self-supporting. The bars hold the design elements together once the background is removed, leaving a lace-like openwork panel.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Richelieu embroidery and cutwork chapters. Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), Richelieu and needle lace bar entries.

content.text: Needle lace bars are worked as part of Richelieu cutwork, a whitework technique in which areas of fabric are cut away after the design outlines and bars are completed. The bars must be made before any cutting takes place, because they need the fabric to be intact for the thread foundations to be laid across. Each bar is a bundle of two or three thread strands stretched across a marked space, then covered from end to end with tight buttonhole stitches so no fabric thread shows through the finished bar. When the surrounding background is cut away with small sharp scissors, the bars hold the remaining design shapes together. The technique requires accurate cutting and confidence with

items.label: Thread
items.value: Coton a broder no. 16 or 25, or pearl cotton no. 12; the thread must be strong enough to hold its structure after the background is removed. White on white linen is traditional

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Firm woven linen or cotton, at least 120 thread count; a tight weave supports the outlining and resists fraying at cut edges. Back with a layer of tissue paper or stabiliser while working to prevent distortion

items.label: Needle
items.value: Embroidery needle size 8 for laying foundation threads and working buttonhole bars; small sharp scissors with fine points for cutting the background

items.label: Hoop
items.value: 20 cm hoop or slate frame; the fabric must remain taut throughout

content.text: Outline the design first. All the outer edges of the design shapes must be finished in padded satin stitch or closely-worked buttonhole stitch before the bars are begun. The outline encloses the fabric that will remain; any fabric outside the outline on the bar side will eventually be cut away.

Lay the bar foundations. Bring the needle up at point (A) on one edge of the space to be bridged. Carry the thread across to point (B) on the opposite edge and take the needle down into the fabric there. Come up very close to (B) again. Carry the thread back to (A) and repeat, so there are 2 or 3 parallel thread strands lying across the space. These strands must be taut but not so tight that they distort the fabric.

Cover the bar with buttonhole stitch. Without entering the fabric, work close buttonhole stitches along the full length of the foundation strands. Hold the strands together with the thumb of the non-working hand so they stay parallel. Each buttonhole loop passes under all the foundation strands and the loop edge faces the same direction throughout. Pull each stitch firmly so the stitches pack tightly and no strand shows beneath.

When the bar is fully covered, take the needle through the fabric at the far end to secure the bar, then travel through the outline edge or the back of the fabric to the start position of the next bar. Work all bars before cutting.

Cut the background. When all bars and outlines are complete, use fine-pointed scissors to cut away the background fabric from each space, cutting close to the outline edge without snipping the bars or the outline stitches. Work from the wrong side where possible to see the stitching clearly.

attrs.heading: When needle lace bars go wrong

items.symptom: The bar sags or loses its shape after the background is cut
items.cause: Too few foundation strands were laid, or the buttonhole stitches were not packed tightly enough to make the bar rigid.
items.fix: Lay at least 3 foundation strands. Work the buttonhole stitches as close together as possible so the bar is solid along its full length. Test a bar by pressing it gently before cutting: it should feel firm, not springy.

items.symptom: The background fabric frays at the cut edges
items.cause: The outer outline stitching was not worked close enough to the cutting line, or the scissors cut into the outline rather than beside it.
items.fix: Ensure the outer outlines are fully worked and completely cover the fold line before cutting. Cut a small amount at a time with the tip of the scissors, and always cut away from the bar and outline stitching.

items.symptom: Buttonhole loops on the bar face different directions
items.cause: The working direction changed partway along the bar.
items.fix: Work always from the same end of the bar to the other without reversing. Keep the loop edge consistently facing the same side of the bar throughout.
